transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-02 15:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Li (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (NimbleDocs Head of Platform), Ravi Kumar (SRE), Leanne Cho (ML Eng)
Links shared: demo deck https://redwood.ai/decks/nimbledocs-edge, benchmark sheet (sheet link), security checklist (link)

Summary: Quick demo of long-context behavior under high TPS, streaming backpressure and how Redwood handles session timeouts and stream-shedding. Showed Console metrics, Optimize recommendations, and a canary fallback to smaller model with partial streaming.
Topics: long-context memory/KV cache evictions, streaming partials and SSE vs websocket, shed policies, timeouts, retry semantics, observable fields in Console, canary rollbacks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we set aside 45 to 60, want to run through the edge-case demo we discussed. Jonah will drive the load tests and console walkthrough.
[00:18] Sara: Perfect, thanks. Quick context - we're seeing spikes up to 6k QPS on certain endpoints, and some sessions persist for, like, 45 to 60 minutes with a couple hundred kilobytes of conversation state.
[00:32] Jonah: Ok, so key things we'll validate are what happens when the KV cash, sorry cache, grows and starts evicting mid-session, and how streaming behaves when the serving pool gets saturated. We'll also show the Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization.
[00:50] Ravi: Two quick constraints: we must keep latency p99 under 500ms for fast endpoints and we have a hard SLA that sessions not be dropped silently — we need audit logs. Also we run in a VPC and need KMS integration.
[01:05] Jonah: Totally. We have a private deployment option for that. For the demo — first we'll spin up a synthetic workload: long-context chats with 50k token histories and a bursty arrival pattern to exercise backpressure.
[01:20] (sound of keyboard)
[01:28] Jonah: Starting the load now — you'll see the Requests/s ramp in Console.
[01:35] Maya: Note, we have the streaming window open — you'll see partial events in the stream when backpressure kicks in.
[01:42] [02:00] Console: Requests/s (graph) 0 -> 6k, pool utilization 92%
[02:12] Leanne: When you say partial events, do you mean we get a partial token chunk and then it's terminated? How is that surfaced to the app?
[02:20] Jonah: Good question. We stream chunks as they generate; if the runtime needs to shed, it will emit a terminal 'partial' event plus a reason code (shed_high_qps or kv_eviction). The client SDK then sees "stream_end_reason" and you can choose to retry or fetch a compacted response.
[02:45] Sara: That's helpful. What's the retry semantics? We can't double-charge users for long responses.
[02:52] Jonah: We expose idempotency tokens and a resume token. For long contexts we recommend resume token + prefix KV cache so you avoid re-computing earlier tokens. There's also a cost-control setting in Console to avoid re-generation if it would exceed a token budget.
[03:15] Ravi: We had an incident where sessions timed out and the UI showed an empty response. How would Redwood prevent a silent drop?
[03:22] Maya: Two layers: first, the client SDK surfaces explicit error states with codes. Second, Console has trace logs and a session timeline — you can map request id to the trace and see whether we returned partial or dropped.
[03:35] Jonah: Let me show the request timeline: here's a sample trace — you can see initial accept, KV fetch, generation start, then a shed event at 18s when memory pressure peaked.
[03:50] [04:05] Jonah: Note there's a mis-ordered timestamp due to clock skew in the synthetic worker but you still get the sequence of events.
[04:12] Leanne: On the client side, is SSE recommended or websocket for streaming resilience?
[04:18] Jonah: SSE is simpler for retries but lacks multiplexing. For high concurrency websocket is better because you can keep a single connection and multiplex multiple session streams. But you must handle backpressure on your socket layer — Redwood's SDK provides backoff helpers.
[04:40] Sara: Can we control shed thresholds? E.g., we want to prioritize authenticated premium users.
[04:45] Jonah: Yes — routing policies let you prioritize by token, route, or model. You can set soft and hard thresholds: soft triggers signal to the runtime to start partial responses, hard triggers forcibly shed lower-priority sessions. We'll demo a canary where we fall back to a smaller model for low-priority users.
[05:05] (demo noise)
[05:18] Jonah: Flipping to Optimize tab — here's a recommendation: increase batch size from 8 to 16 for this model shape which reduces p95 CPU but may add 20ms to median. Optimize also suggested a 4-bit quantized variant for non-premium traffic to save ~45% tokens cost.
[05:40] Ravi: Any quality regression monitoring? We cannot degrade understanding on important flows.
[05:45] Maya: Yes we tie regr alerts to eval sets; Optimize will surface a per-prompt BLEU-ish delta and you can set automatic rollback on blur above threshold.
[05:58] Sara: Show us failover to smaller model flow please.
[06:05] Jonah: Canary rule: if pool saturation > 85% for 30s, route new requests from route X to model-small-v2, and stream an informational partial to the client explaining degraded fidelity.
[06:22] [06:40] Console: Canary switch executed at 06:21, route X -> model-small-v2
[06:28] Leanne: How does KV cache eviction play with model switch? Will the smaller model have a different KV encoding?
[06:35] Jonah: Great catch — we keep shared KV formats where possible; when model families change we do a compacted migration: we store a compact prefix representation and the runtime can map it. There is a small mismatch window; Optimize will warn when that risk is non-zero.
[06:55] Sara: Are we going to lose long-term context if the cache evicts?
[07:00] Jonah: If the cache evicts older context, we provide a compaction API: you can store a summary token that represents the earlier history. The demo includes automatic summarization as part of the shed policy.
[07:14] (unintelligible whisper)
[07:22] Maya: Quick pivot — I'm going to start a high-frequency burst test to show timeouts.
[07:30] Jonah: Starting burst - note the stream shows an increasing queue depth and then we hit per-model concurrency limit resulting in queue TTLs expiring.
[07:42] Console: queue TTL expire events at 07:41:23 (reason: concurrency_exceeded)
[07:48] Ravi: At what point do we observe user-facing timeouts versus retriable server-side errors?
[07:55] Jonah: We return 429 with a Retry-After header for short-term backpressure; if the request exceeds queue TTL we send 499 client_cancelled-like semantics to let you know it didn't finish. Nothing is silently dropped.
[08:10] Leanne: Can we adjust queue TTLs per route?
[08:14] Jonah: Yes per-route TTLs and per-route concurrency caps. You can also define preemption for premium routes that tear down low-priority queued items.
[08:30] Sara: Walk me through an example flow where a session resumes after a shed.
[08:36] Jonah: Example: client receives stream_end with resume_token R123. Client calls /resume with R123; runtime fetches cached KV blocks and continues from last generated token. If compacted summary exists it'll insert that to keep sequence length bounded.
[08:50] [09:05] Maya: There's a small demo note: some words in the demo may be transcribed as "sam-el" instead of SAML in the recordings, ignore that.
[09:12] Ravi: Security — we need to ensure audit logs tie to our SSO principal.
[09:18] Maya: We map request ids to SAML user_urn in our logs; for Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM-backed keys and full audit export. We'll attach SOC2 and ISO artifacts to the follow up.
[09:35] Leanne: For on-prem, what's the rollback story if the canary causes correctness regressions?
[09:42] Jonah: Canary is controlled via rollout policy; console allows instant rollback and automatic rollback triggers on eval regressions. We also keep warm standby replicas for quick fallback.
[09:55] Sara: Can you show the raw stream payload for a partial event?
[10:00] Jonah: Sure — here's a sample event: {"type":"partial","tokens":"...","stream_end_reason":"shed_high_qps","resume_token":"R123","cost_estimate":"12 tokens"} (rounded for demo).
[10:18] Maya: Ok, next we'll run a combined long-context + burst where we purposely bump the KV eviction threshold to see effects.
[10:25] Jonah: Increasing eviction aggressiveness now.
[10:30] Console: KV eviction events spike, generation latency p99 increases, shed events increase.
[10:40] Leanne: I'm seeing weird truncation in output where a sentence ends mid-word in the UI. Is that a transcription artifact?
[10:48] Jonah: That's expected when a partial stream is cut due to shed — depending on where tokens were flushed you might get mid-token cut. We recommend the SDK to apply token-level smoothing or re-request the remainder with resume token.
[11:05] Sara: For billing, how are partial responses billed? We need clarity for customer support.
[11:12] Maya: Billing is per-token generated; partials are billed for tokens that were actually produced. We provide a per-request token breakdown in Console and via the billing API so you can reconcile.
[11:30] Ravi: Ok, for the pilot we'd want: 1) a 24-hour test with our traffic profile, 2) full trace logs and p99 samples, 3) a security review if we go beyond PoC.
[11:40] Maya: Sounds good. We'll configure a dedicated test pool with a small reserved capacity and a burst buffer so you can validate SLA behaviors.
[11:50] Jonah: I'll package the load generator configs and the exact console filters.
[12:02] (overlap/crosstalk)
[12:10] Maya: Quick recap — Maya to send pricing and pilot plan; Jonah to send load configs and KV trace examples; Ravi to share QPS histogram and any internal SSO mapping requirements. We target kickoff next week.
[12:25] Sara: Thanks, this was useful.
[12:30] End.
